utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second-to-last paragraph. Can you see that: "We do not accept ..."

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm interested in the last sentence of that paragraph: "We inform all Serbs, whose houses have been burnt and destroyed, that they can come back to the liberated territory. In Baranja only, there are 17 villages to be populated." So you weren't familiar that kind of --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a -- what's the date of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was only there for three weeks at the end of October and November, and it was dark and it was cold, and there was a lot of shelling. So I didn't really -- I don't even think I went into the town. It was awful.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What's interesting, Mrs. Celar, is, on the one hand, you have these discriminatory policies that I just showed you, getting people out of their jobs and out of the -- the Baranja area, and, at the same time, inviting Serb refugees to come in.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a -- it's not a situation that I either knew about or thought about at that time, or I would have spoken up about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to talk briefly about the Ratkajec family.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ratkajec.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ratkajec family. That you discuss in your -- in your statement. Was there more than one Ratkajec family in the area?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could have been. It was a particular one that I knew that were living in the area where -- there were two families in the -- well, there were two houses in their garden in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know their first names at all?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now. There was -- grandmother, grandfather, wife, her husband gone to Osijek, and the two boys.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In one house?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The new house belonged to the mother with their two sons, and the other house was the grandfather and grandmother; they lived there. But I think they moved together eventually to live together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In one house?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the bigger of the houses. Excuse me, this was a -- in the big house, they had a flat upstairs as well. I think this -- so I would imagine at some time the family -- it appeared that the family had been down stairs and upstairs was a separate flat, and then they built the house in the garden.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Does the street Franza Liszta sound familiar. Is that where they lived?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know it was near the November the 20th Street, very close to there, but I can't actually tell you the name of their straight.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you don't know -- you don't remember the exact street in which they lived.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not there, no. We had friends in the November 20th, and they lived a little bit further on the main road. That was sort of a side street and they lived further up on the corner of the two roads, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you were saying that you helped them in April of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- to regulate an issue with the --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I think it was, if I've put it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you say that people from the JNA were placed on roof-tops to try to find the perpetrators who had thrown grenades --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just over the Easter period when they'd been threatened with death. We went to the police who didn't do anything, and so then we went to appeal to General Adzic -- General Krstic who I'd been at those meetings with, and he said he would put two -- just for that -- whether it was one day or two days. I volunteered to go and sleep there. Ilija said that we would patrol the street and make it known that I was sleeping there, and the army promised to put these soldiers to cover that area. For that specific time when the specific threat had been made, which was over Easter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because, according to the information we have, the Ratkajecs, who did live on two properties that were essentially connected, that both houses were inhabited by the family until August 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the information we have is that in August 1992, one of the families they were forced because of explosions and threats to leave their homes --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- in one house and you're saying --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't leave, because Mr. Ratkajec before -- the grandfather told me that before --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm not finished.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That in one house the family with two children, they had to leave in August of 1992. So up until August in 1992 both houses were inhabited by the Ratkajec family.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that it was after August 1992 that the second house was inhabited by Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't actually happen like that. That second house -- I slept in that second house during that Easter time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it was empty according to you?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they sort of used both houses and the grandfather was in -- and grandmother was were in a very, very nervous state. And in fact when the -- and I really think that they moved together because they were frightened. When I went to visit them, they would be sitting in the big house.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. We'll look some more into that.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I thought you meant they'd left the -- the area entirely, that they weren't living in either house anymore. That's what I thought you meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That one of the families living in the house, they were forced out of their house in August of 1992 because of grenades being thrown into their yard and because of threats that they received.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not actually what happened. Because those grenades were. Thrown in -- I went round to see it -- into the kitchen. But it was -- there wasn't a lot of damage, it was a window, and it was repaired. But they were living in both -- they were sleeping more with the grandparents. They felt safer together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In your -- your statement, you describe a lot happening in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you also described these threats and explosions that were happening in April of 1992 in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And it's also around that time that UNPROFOR was supposed to assume responsibility in that area.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you know that there was, in fact, a spike in crimes around the time that UNPROFOR was about to take responsibility for the area?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I remember about that time that before they were -- had their mandate, that they -- there was the big battle and that's where everybody -- there could have been. Yes, because the men were -- it also coincided with the fact that the men from all the families were sent to the front line on the Drava, and the older men were guarding the water installations. And all the women, we were all on our own in the houses. And I think I gave testimony before that that's when I had all my livestock stolen at night, and a shop was broken into and our camera was stolen. That was about that time. Because there was nobody about in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. Are you aware that the violent crimes against non-Serbs spiked around the time that UNPROFOR was about do assume responsibility in the area?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, crime in general, I thought was, stealing from people and trying to steal people's cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you know that this pattern of the escalation of crimes was repeated in areas outside of Baranja did you have any information --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know that in Christmas and Easter of 1992, the Dalj Croats were driven out of their homes and taken to Osijek by bus. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you know that also in Easter of 1992, the Croats and Hungarians were forced onto buses and expelled from Erdut by men in military camouflage?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I had never been in Erdut and I've never been to Dalj, but I knew about Ratkajec and their problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you know about the expulsions of non-Serbs around the same time in places like Dzacovski [phoen], Caric, Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I thought was in Bosnia, Tovarnik. I don't know -- where is that, Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you've never --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's in Bosnia. I don't know. I didn't think it was in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So I'd -- put it to you --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise it, excuse me, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you don't recognise it. I'm putting to you, Mrs. Celar, that you were not in a position to know if Serbs were being mistreated throughout the SBWS showing a pattern of crimes against them; right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You don't know if crimes were being committed against non-Serbs in other places --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- in a similar pattern?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you don't know if there's a pattern in timing of the crimes against non-Serbs in other places and whether it's similar timing to what was happening in Baranja?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Gosnell, re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Celar.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just a few questions to follow up on what has been asked you by the Prosecutor. If we could have, please, 65 ter 6604 on the screen, please. And if we could start with the first page for a few moments and then we'll turn over to page 5 of the English. Do you remember, Mrs. Celar, earlier today having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then, please, if we can go to page 5 in the English. And there's this reference in the letter that appears to have been sent by Ilija Celar to an attorney, to "a decision of 3rd August 2009 concerning suspended criminal proceedings raised against me under Article 120 of the basic criminal law of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then what you were asked at page 31 and then your answer followed was: "Q. So I'm a bit confused about you saying, on the one hand, that all the charges were dismissed in 2006 and here is Ilija Celar asking for the withdrawal of the international arrest warrant." Your answer: "That's right. That's what we did it for because we had to -- in order to get the withdrawal of the Interpol, we had to prove that the warrant was no longer outstanding and that's why he employed the lawyer to go and find out what was happening with the Osijek court. I thought it was 2006 because we were a bit cross that nobody ever told us -- that nobody went to Osijek, and it wasn't in a newspaper." Is it possible - and here's my question - is it possible that rather than it being 2006 it was, in fact, 2009 that you were informed of this?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perfectly possible because one of the dates is wrong, I feel, because Ilija only went to one lawyer to investigate any charges. So either my date is wrong or that date's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please move to page 111 in the B/C/S. And, unfortunately, there is no translation of this in English, so, if I may, I would like to the assistance of my learned colleague to read out a specific portion which we suggest corresponds to the reference on page 5 of the translated portion, and answer that it could be interpreted, of course, by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honour, I would omit about 15 names which are irrelevant for this case, if -- [Interpretation] In the name of the Republic of Croatia, decision, the district court in Osijek, Judge Zvonko Vekic, Presiding Judge in the criminal case against the accused Svetislav Branic et al, because of the crime mentioned in Article 120, paragraph 1, of the basic criminal law of the Republic of Croatia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please slow down when you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "(NN number 31/93, 108/95, and 28/96." Further on: "... OKZ RH) in connection with the indictment issued by the District State Prosecutor's office in Osijek, number KT 136/94, dated the 3rd of April, 2001, on the 3rd of August, 2009 has decided as follows: On the basis of Article 291, paragraph 1, item 2 of the Law on Criminal Procedure (NN number 110/97, 27/98, 58/99, 112/99, 58/02, 148/02 and 115/06, further on referred to as ZKP), is halting criminal proceedings against ... 52, the accused, Ilija Celar ... for the following reasons: In the period between August 1991 and March 1993, in Beli Manastir and other locations in the territory of Baranja, during the armed rebellion of the local Serb population against the constitutional legal order of the Republic of Croatia and attacks of the JNA and paramilitary units from Serbia against the Republic of Croatia, with the intention of establishing an occupation system of government in the area of Baranja, preventing the re-establishment of the Croatian constitutional order, and in order to annex all of Baranja to the so-called Greater Serbia, they joined together and armed and with military equipment, together with several other rebels during the course of August 1991, at first, took part in the establishment of a para-police body of government, the so-called Secretariat for Internal Affairs, Beli Manastir, and the toppling and persecution of legal local organs of government. Furthermore, as members of the aforementioned secretariat, namely, the accused [In English]. I omit all the names but the name of Ilija Celar. "... as members of the special-purposes unit [In English] "Ilija Celar ..." the other names after him [Interpretation] "... as members of the so-called police pursuant to orders issued to them by their superiors, carried out ungrounded searches of houses and apartments, which were illegal, as well as the arrests of the civilian population of Baranja of non-Serb ethnicity. They also brought in prisoners to the premises of the aforementioned secretariat, they questioned the prisoners, all the while insulting them and ill-treating them physically and mentally. They intimidated the non-Serbian population of Baranja and they confiscated valuable assets. Therefore, they participated in the armed rebellion which was aimed at undermining the constitutional state order and/or security of the Republic of Croatia. And, in that way, committed a crime against the Republic of Croatia - around rebellion - as described and punishable pursuant to Article 235, paragraph 1, of the penal code of the Republic of Croatia. "Statement of reasons: By the indictment issued of -- by the county prosecutor's office in Osijek, number KT 1936/94 dated 3 April 2001, Svetislav Branic and others (a total of 58 accused) were charged for crimes against humanity and the international law, war crime against a civilian population pursuant to Article 120, paragraph 1, of the penal code of the Republic of Croatia. "On 16 July 2009, the county prosecutor's office in Osijek issued a document and changed the factual and legal description of the indictment with regard to the accused listed in the preamble of this decision, thereby charging them with committing a crime against the Republic of Croatia - armed rebellion - pursuant to Article 235, paragraph 1, of the penal code of the Republic of Croatia. "At the same time, by the same document, the county's prosecutor's office from Osijek has suggested that by applying Articles 1 and 2, paragraph 2, of the Law on General Pardon, the proceedings against the aforementioned accused should be stopped. "Since, in the preamble of this decision, the aforementioned accused have been charged with a crime of armed rebellion, pursuant to Article 235, paragraph 1 of the penal code of the Republic of Croatia, which has been comprised by the Law on General Pardon (NN number 80/96), this court has established that the proposal of the county state prosecutor's office from Osijek is granted, and that there are hindrances obstructing the continuation of the proceedings pursuant Article 353, paragraph 6, of the Law on Criminal Proceedings." [In English] I believe it is the relevant part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Celar, that was -- that was quite a lengthy legal discussion, but I just want to try, if I may, to highlight a couple of aspects of it and see if it jogs your memory about whether any of these things were mentioned by Ilija Celar to you. And the first aspect is do you recall whether he mentioned to you that there had been any recommendation by the prosecutor in Osijek county to drop the charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't actually understand what the question is, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me situate this in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, your microphone, please. It's okay now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps can I situate this in respect of your answer to the Prosecution -- to a question and it was at page 29, line 21. It's not on the page in front of you, Mrs. Celar, it's what you said earlier today --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And leaving aside the date, you said it was your recollection that Ilija Celar had been found not guilty?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And now what I'm attempting to do is explore a little further and I'm asking whether, did you also hear from Ilija Celar whether preceding a final determination on being found not guilty do you remember whether he mentioned that the charges were recommended to be dropped by the Croatian authorities? And you may not remember that at all but I'm just asking if that --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember a lot about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you recall whether Ilija Celar had a document with him or received a document pertaining to any of this --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? Recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the time-period when he informed you about the charges either being dropped or being found not guilty.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information came back from the lawyer and from other people on that list. They rang first and then I think he confirmed it with his lawyer. Excuse me, I don't think he had a lawyer then. They rang him and said that there'd been a decision, and then Ilija wanted to clarify what had been happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You just said that he heard from other people on that list --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you -- do I understand correctly, then, that you mean other people telephoned him having heard about this --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- development?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you ever learn whether the Interpol arrest warrant was, in fact, suppressed or he was removed from any --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it. I read their notification. I've read the -- and helped him write the letter that said, Here is my paperwork from -- it's a different paper to this. Through the lawyer, he got something which confirmed there were no outstanding charges against him and we sent that paperwork to France. And then France replied and said they would investigate. And I think it was six months later he got a letter to say that they had removed his name from the -- their red list there because they had nothing to -- they'd checked and there was nothing that they had -- no request to arrest him. Something -- terminology like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when you say that he received this document through the lawyer, that he got something, was that something from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At today's transcript earlier this -- this morning at page 38, you were discussing having spoken to Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you said that you were speaking to Mr. Zivanovic in the context of the troubles that the Ratkajec family were having.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you said that he said to you that it wasn't possible to go on the radio as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah -- well, I don't know whether he meant the radio or it wasn't possible to change what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you explain a little more fully --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the impression he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- what it was, Mrs. Celar -- and just wait until the end of my question or else it won't be transcribed and translated. Did he tell you anything else on that occasion or explain more fully what he meant?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave him quite a talking to and Ilija translated it so there wasn't any misinterpretation of what I was saying. And I thought he was sort of a powerless name. I don't know whether he cared or not, but he just shrugged really and said, I can't do anything. My impression was that he was ineffective. At that moment, what I was asking him for, he wouldn't give me any reassurances at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And why wouldn't -- what was your impression of why he wouldn't give you those reassurances?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he could control what was happening because the actions that were in -- in -- in my opinion, having not seen any of these orders, I really thought that the actions being carried out against Croatians was by criminals because they only targeted people with big houses or big cars, and my opinion was that they were a criminal undertaking that was carrying out these acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we now have, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, before we move to something else -- Mrs. Celar, when your husband was translating or interpreting what you said in English in Serbian to Mr. Zivanovic, did you understand what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood the -- my grammar is appalling in Serbian but I can generally understand 95 per cent of what is said in the terminology. I just don't know how to implement the male and female gender variations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we now have 06568, which is Prosecution tab 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Celar, this is coming up on screen in front of you, the transcript of your television interview which was shown to you yesterday. Do you remember being shown that?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we please could go to page 2. There's a portion where you are recorded as -- transcribed as having said: "I believe that Tudjman is capable of sacrificing his own refugees as a excuse to attack us. I know it is hard to leave your house but many of the local Croats were living in German-owned houses for being good Communists." And then you described or responded to a question from the Prosecution and this starts at page 10.948, line 9, and you were asked some questions which I will not go over here because you -- it's already recorded. But you mentioned it was also a time and I'm quoting of "tremendously stressful that time, very stressful that time." And then you are reminded or the Prosecution says to you that this is September 1992. Now, what I'm interested in is that first sentence of the two from the transcript where you say: "I believe that Tudjman is capable of sacrificing his own refugees as an excuse to attack us," why - if you recall - did you say that at the time? What is the connection between the two?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot understand why I said that. Taken in the whole of what I was saying then was -- the whole emphasis of my letters to newspapers was to, I thought that the -- most of people were in ignorance of the history of the area and that it was a very strong feeling of Serbs that -- I'll repeat it again. It's not being against ethnic groups. They just really believed it was part of Serbia. And it seemed to be at that time that there was tremendous bias against Serbia. I know there was paranoia, but everybody really believed that places like Germany were against Serbia and that the plan for Croatia to do what it did had been long in the making. And everybody in Baranja thought -- the Serbs that I knew and talked to, and my husband. Felt defensive, not as if they were the aggressors. And it seemed to be an awful injustice the way things were being reported outside. But I can't answer the -- why I said that, I have no idea. I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have, please, 65 ter 05259.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, is there a tab number for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There's no tab number.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- I don't believe I received notice that the Defence would be using this in re-direct, so if I could have an opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just to note here for the record, Mr. President, that the issue of notice of documents on re-direct was litigated during the presentation of the Prosecution case, in particular, in respect of Witness GH168, a transcript reference page is page 8519. Documents were presented to that witness on re-direct with no notice to the Defence. Objections were raised, they were resisted by the Prosecution, and then those objections were overruled. And I'm guided by that -- by those rulings in presenting this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear Ms. Biersay objecting, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Quite right, Mr. President. I simply wanted to explain why I have proceeded in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That would then have given a little bit of time to Ms. Biersay to look into the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I proceed or should I wait?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Sorry. If could I have just 90 seconds, I'd be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is a document which is dated 26 September 1992. The front page doesn't concern you, Mrs. Celar, but if we could turn over to page 2. And I'll read from this memorandum which appears to have been recording a conversation between officials of UNPROFOR and officials of Croatia. And it says: "There were two brigades of special police in Sector East that had not been disarmed; therefore, Sector East cannot be considered as having been demilitarised." Then it talks about de-mining. "And the Vance Plan does not allow for consideration of the return of the refugees until security could be guaranteed. He" -- and this appears to be a reference, just for your information to the UNPROFOR sector commander: "He then cited two documents to further demonstrate that the situation in Sector East is such that the return of the refugees can not be allowed now. These documents were the release concerning the meeting of the Secretary-General and President Tudjman and his order from the Force Commander. "He continued by emphasizing that the return of the refugees was the responsibility of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and that the return will be conducted in an orderly manner, and that than UNPROFOR will assist UNHCR, especially with security arrangements." Then if we could move, please, to page 3. Mr. Glavas, do you know who -- -

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh yes I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I met him socially at first. He used to use the same restaurant as us. He used to play cards there. And then when we left, I heard that he was -- I don't know exactly his position but sort of the mayor. When I first knew him, he didn't have any position at all. In Osijek I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He was the mayor of what?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Osijek, I think. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas replied that the Croatian civilians -- and here I'm not going to read the entire thing, but he's talking about essentially some refugees being returned to Baranja, non-Serb or Croatian refugees: "Mr. Glavas replied that the Croatian civilians will be accompanied by police and civil authorities will take charge. He was not asking a return to villages that had been populated 50-50 per cent, but to villages that had been 100 per cent Croatian. He was insisting on return to only four villages in Beli Manastir, to Bilje only at this time. Now if we can turn to the third -- or the fourth page of this document in e-court that last point about Bilje is specifically addressed. "Point 3, (return to villages suggested and picked by the refugees) while sounding attractive, could be quite dangerous. If Bilje is handed over, would that mean that the boundary would be pushed back into Baranja since Croatian police - armed - would be empowered, as suggested to assume law and order functions? Similarly, if the four contiguous villages to the south were secured for them, would that also mean that a substantial tract would that similarly carved out? Then step by step, Croatia would retake parts of its territory." My question is, and it relates back to what you said during your interview when you said: "I believe that Tudjman is capable of sacrificing his own refugees as an excuse to attack us." My question ask does this --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have related to this. It could have related to that if it was a force -- well, not force, but bringing people back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you aware of these -- or the proposal to have Croatian police --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- armed Croatian police accompany the return of refugees to Baranja at the time were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- we discussed that because this is when we started talking about leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was that prospect something that you were alarmed by?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when -- I feared a return by the Croatian forces because to say I didn't think they would come in an orderly manner is true. I never thought that they'd come in -- I thought they -- my neighbour warned me. My Croatian neighbour, Ella said to me, and I never forgot it, on 3rd of April when the attack was happening -- in some strange way the telephones between Osijek and Beli Manastir worked for a long time. Anyway she had a message that we had to go and hide in the kukura [phoen], in the corn fields. The stalks were all brown. They hadn't harvested them that year. So she came to me and said, Amanda, you must come and we'll go and hide in the corn fields. And I said well, can we take everybody? And really, why? And she said, because when they come, they're going to kill everybody here. And that was a -- I believed her because she was a Croatian lady. So then I made mad plans of putting as many people in it the street I could into my house and trying to find an English flag and was going to go out -- all I'd got was a cup. It sounds funny now, but it was terrifying at the time, to say go out and say, they're all English. They're all my family. So we never had an impression that a return by Croatian forces without the control of the UN or -- was something to -- that we would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document 05259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Celar, thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Celar, where do you live now? And when I say "you," I mean you and your husband.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia, in Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us - I think it's page 72 of the transcript of that day - that your husband was a member of special forces and that they were something in between 17 to 46 of them --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- the exact numbers are not important. And it was a group of people who came together to see how they could defend themselves; right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This group of people, did they stay on their own or did they, sooner or later, incorporate in some other structure?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may explain. At the beginning, as I understood it, they were people from different villages, and they met in Beli Manastir, like us from Osijek, where we'd moved, and they met to discuss what was happening in their areas and how they could protect themselves, and those were 19 original members. Then, on that first night, they were surrounded and attacked by Croatian police and one of them was killed. And that left 18. Due to the tremendous amount of gun-fire, other Serbs came and joined in, and in the end, I -- Ilija told me the numbers were something like 46 men grouped together, and I think there was something like 1500 Croatian police. But the Croatian police thought there were far more of then. That was the initial group who didn't join anybody else. People joined them. This was in the first -- I could say three weeks of -- from April the 19th, 1991 up to, maybe, early September. That's my understanding of what -- those men. Then eventually, I think they were incorporated into whatever else was -- they changed uniforms and joined and patrolled the front lines. But I don't -- I don't know -- other people were required to join. The people men who lived in Baranja of fighting age were required to join or dig ditches if they didn't want to fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So if I understand well, you don't really know whether they were incorporated in some other structure TO or --

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Or they were not?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know categorically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Where did they get uniforms witness weapons from.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they initially had blue uniforms like the police uniform, I think. But I wasn't there, so I didn't see what they were wearing. I saw them in the October, when they were wearing blue. I don't know where their guns came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I have one more question, but I see the time. We'll take the second break for 30 minutes, and, after the break, I still have one question for you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For my next and last question, I would ask to have on the screen exhibit number P3039, 3-0-3-9. Mrs. Celar, this is a document which has been shown to you by the Prosecution. Ms. Biersay, could you remind us, the context of this document it is a letter written by whom to whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can read it from the first -- from the -- from the -- the first page of the document. It's the Hungarian minister of foreign affairs to Mr. Hans Van den Broek, president of the Council of Ministers of the European Community; right? And it's dated 18 October 1991. And I would like you, Mrs. Celar, to read the entire second page. So if we could have the second page. And you tell me when you finished reading.

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would like to put your statement, paragraph 81, in the context of this information given by the Hungarian minister of foreign affairs. Your statement was that you knew that there were many Hungarian people living in Baranja and you didn't know about one of them leaving or having to leave. That's you're statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. How do you contextualise this?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the villages in here weren't in the part where I was. I was mainly in Beli Manastir, and the villages I visited, which were Hungarian, were Batina, by the bridge, Knezevi Vinograd some of the other villages. I can't remember the Hungarian villages that were mainly Hungarian in those areas. I know there were and I know I went there. The one example I went was when I went to fetch the goat. Most of the Hungarian that lived there spoke Hungarian, not Serbo-Croat. So I wouldn't have communicated with them in that event. I would have needed a translator. My husband doesn't speak Hungarian. I simply never wasn't aware. I knew Croats were leaving, and I knew the criminality that was going on. But one of -- I don't remember who said it to me, but one of people I knew said that Hungarians lived in their villages and didn't much care who governed them as long as they left them alone. They weren't interested in either Croatia or Serbia, that they had their own villages. I can't be much more -- I mean, I didn't set out to investigate who'd been -- I didn't investigate who'd been set out or ... it simply -- I didn't undertake any sort of mission like that. I was trying to live on a daily basis at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that with regard to all this information that your -- your knowledge was rather limited?

utterances.speaker: AMANDA CELAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was limited when I was in Beli Manastir. I -- I had more strong opinions when I was in Osijek because I met more people that had been affected and I was personally affected in Osijek. But when I went to Baranja, I didn't really very often go outside what you would call the city limits because really it was too dangerous go in anywhere. And I occasionally went to Jagodnjak to visit my mother-in-law there, but I didn't. I -- I -- I -- yes, I would agree with you. It was limited in regards of I knew what orders were being given or carried out or expulsions, et cetera. The only thing could I witness was who came into -- the refugees that coming in that we were greeting, where they were coming from, well the ones I saw. Not the ones going to villages, I didn't know who they were. I never met them. I know when I organised 280 packages of -- from Britain, humanitarian aid, we instruct the Red Cross chief, Zeljko Cengi, and I agreed that the packages would not stay in Beli Manastir, that every single village would receive some of these packages with the exceptions of the books for the schools, the notebooks and pencils for schools.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Celar. This brings your testimony to an end. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal with your testimony. Are you now released as a witness, and the court usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the court usher will escort you out of the courtroom, and we wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I rise to discuss some housekeeping matters pertaining to some documents relating to this witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The first is the video that the Defence used on re-direct and that I used on cross, specifically 65 ter 6568, which is the video of her giving an interview to Serbian television, and we would like to tender that as 65 ter number 6568.1. So just the clip that was shown. So we tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: There's no objection to that but I'm not sure I understand whether the transcript is also being tendered and I would say that it ought to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's protocol that when we upload the video, we also have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 06568.1 will be Exhibit P3245.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I understand that we'll need access to change -- to add the .1 to the -- to the 65 ter number. But that's something that with can discuss the Registry. The second issue is I have consulted with Mr. Gosnell, and I have reiterated the request that we get the document about which Mrs. Celar testified, the 2006 document that was sent to her husband. So we have agreement that we -- we will request that from her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's the one Mr. Zivanovic read in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, that's the one we don't have. She said there was a document given to her husband that dates from 2006, and so we -- it's unclear what the document is but we've asked for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And it's very unclear whether it is a 2006 document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Exactly. So in any event, we've requested whatever document shes that, that she's discussing, that we have it. And this is linked to the third point I have, which we would like to tender the convictions at later date, once we have more information. And I have discussed this with Mr. Gosnell who assures with me that he is not agreeing in advance to any admission of the document but he will not object to the timeliness of the tendering of the document, which we will do at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We understand. And that -- Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just for the record and just to make this clear and also subject to the reservation that we would have the opportunity to tender other portions of 65 ter 06604 that may be relevant to the documents being tendered by the Prosecution that are also part of that same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That 65 ter number you are citing is the -- the -- the large volume of documents you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- the OTP got from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've broken it up into two so 6603 is one set and 6604 but I completely agree with Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and perhaps also you ask for a copy for -- to be delivered to you by the witness. I think it -- it would be appropriate to instruct the witness, and I'm sure the Registrar will convey the message to VWS, that it would be transferred through VWS.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. Thank you. That terminates my -- my intervention, and with the Court's permission, I would seek leave to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please do. Have a nice day. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Unless you need Ms. Biersay to be here? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can Ms. Biersay leave the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As far as you are concerned? Okay. I see -- just one moment. I see Mr. Stringer is not here anymore but that is not a problem. On -- on Monday, and I'm sorry, I -- I -- I had a little note on my office desk to -- with the -- with the exhibit numbers but I left it, so I have to do it off the top of my head without the numbers then. On Monday, there is a document that has been MFI'd, pending -- pending a reservation from Mr. Zivanovic who asked Serbia whether the document was complete. On the 3rd of September - so that would have been yesterday, I think - that same document has been admitted. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The MFI is P3231. And the admitted one, same document, is 3242. P numbers. Now, what I will do is vacate, ask the Registrar to vacate the MFI number. We keep the -- the admitted one P3242, as admitted. And if the information you get from - I think it was Serbia, Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If the information you get would cause a problem, you'll have to file a motion eventually to add -- parts of documents or whatever. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's your turn, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. Your Honour, we have one -- we got this morning one information related to the witness DGH-044. He is scheduled to testify on Monday, and he is under subpoena of this Trial Chamber. He called my -- my investigator and told her that his mother has health problem. She had a stroke last night and that he was not able to travel as -- as scheduled. He had to come to The Hague tomorrow. And he -- he asked if he could testify through videolink but we cannot see him -- anything -- any -- any -- any response to -- to such request. It is just our information. We'll -- I -- I like to convey this information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and we'll provide for you if -- if he find any documents to support his -- his statement, we'll provide it at earliest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think you should -- you should proceed by filing a motion to solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll do it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing else? Then we can call the next witness. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. It is appropriate time for the next witness to inform the Chamber that it is my intention to use four documents that the witness provided me during the proofing sessions, and I informed the Prosecution about it. These documents are not yet the Rule 65 ter list but we'll file my -- our motion to amend or Rule 65 ter list with this these four documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Has the OTP a position?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I just want to inquire with Mr. Zivanovic, because a list was updated this morning, and there are five document, not four. Can you just confirm the 65 ter numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. I wanted to say for the fifth document, separately. But I'll give the numbers of these documents. These are 1D3744, 1D3745, 1D3746, and 1D3747.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honour, at this stage we do not have an objection to their addition to the 65 ter list, and we reserve our objections on admissibility at a later stage. And I believe there's a fifth document. Is this also something that is going to be raised in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we found one document. It is 1D3749. It is document provided in the earlier -- earlier -- from one of the Prosecution witnesses. I think it was GH-102. And we would use some parts of this document. It is just a one-page document. If there is no objection, we -- we would use this document too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will have to consult that document first because on your list it's 1D3727. So I haven't had the opportunity to look at 3749 quite yet, but before the end of the session I will have a look and state my position. But as I said, Your Honour, there's no objection to the four documents announced so far to be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So for those four, and I think the numbers are on record, you may add them to your 65 ter list, Mr. Zivanovic. And the fifth one, we will hear from the OTP at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we now call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Trial Chamber. First of all, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Vojislav Vukcevic. I was born on the 4th of July, 1938.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to that you the solemn declaration does expose you to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. So could I ask you to read now the solemn declaration the usher -- the court usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Zivanovic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukcevic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Although we know each other, for the record, I'm going to introduce myself to you. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I represent Goran Hadzic in these proceedings. Mr. Vukcevic, you gave a statement, a written statement, to Mr. Hadzic's Defence team a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have, please, 1D2401.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement will appear on the screen for your benefit. It seems that we don't have a signed version of your statement. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Zivanovic, the Registrar tells me that this is the unsigned version and that the signed versions -- version is .1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. It is an error from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would you need --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But we have the signed version too. I -- at the moment, I'm not able to tell you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, it's the same number, .1. So perhaps we should call that one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's the same -- the same statement but it was -- I have the signed statement and I have it in hard copy too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have the signed statement on the screen. If that's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would give to -- to the witness the -- the signed version of his statement in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh. We have it on the screen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please now look at your screen. Do you recognise your signature on this statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether, on the second page --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my signature is on the second page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the remaining three pages? First the third page.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my signature is on the third page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: I can see my signature on the last page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, you will perhaps remember that we had an interview here in The Hague after your arrival. You wanted us to make some corrections in the statement. The first one is paragraph 8 on page 4. That's in the original version. And in the English version, it will be the penultimate paragraph on page 4. In that part of your statement it says that you lived in Baranja until the 4th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You wanted to change the date and you wanted to give us correct date until which you lived in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: I lived there until 6th of September. This is a typo. I lived in Baranja until the 6th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph of this statement, you also mentioned an attack against the barracks in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when that happened.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: I was a full-time professor at the school of law in Osijek. On the 2nd of September, 1991, there -- the -- that -- that was when the exam term was. I decided to spend the night in Osijek because I had a flat there where I could actually spend the night. And that's what I did. Earlier dawn, and I can't remember the exact time, I was woken up by the shell explosions resounding all over the city. I got up. I switched on the radio to listen to the local Osijek station. I wanted to hear what was going on. And then I heard some words that I had never heard before. The radio informed the listeners that the Serbian Chetnik armada had attacked the city of Osijek and that the citizens would be well advised not to leave their apartments until further notice. It was also stated that members of the national guard which was just a different name for the 1st Corps of the newly established Croatian state and who were also known under the popular nickname Zenga were in conflict with members of the Chetnik armada. To took me a few moments to grasp what I was on what was going on. I had never heard that there was something as Serbian Chetnik armada. It was a terrible thing to hear those words. And then the anchor continued reporting as if from a sporting event that members of the Croatian army had put up defence against that armada by opening fire on the barracks in the lower part of the city of Osijek, which was just across the street from the hospital. He also said that fierce fighting was underway between members of the Croatian guards and members of the occupying Yugoslav People's Army. A cannon shell was fired from somewhere. I don't know what its calibre was because I don't know anything about those elements and about that. And inflicted the first casualty on the day, and the day was the 3rd of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the last paragraph of your statement, on the last page, you also made a correction, or several corrections.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph, there is a reference to a person whose name was Kresojevic and he was from Bobetko and you spoke about him with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you can see that. Could you please tell us about that Kresojevic from Bobeta what party was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Kresojevic had been a fully fledged member of the SPS which is the abbreviation for the Socialist Party of Serbia, the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So not of the SDS as we can read in the statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It arises from that paragraph that you discussed a speech of his with Goran Hadzic. Tell me, please, on that occasion when you spoke, was Kresojevic also in the car or was he absent or, rather, was he not in the car?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not in the car. Goran Hadzic and I talked on the way to Knin. We went there frequently because Knin was the seat of the Serbian Democratic Party for Croatia. On that occasion, Goran Hadzic said that the speech that had been delivered by Kresojevic in Belgrade and in which he said that Serbs from Eastern Slavonia fully supported Milosevic was not true and that Kresojevic did it on his own without consulting anybody. I have to tell you that a lot of courage was needed to say something bad about Slobodan Milosevic. You had to be very certain about your collocutor and had you to be sure that you would not suffer consequences as a result of such words. Goran Hadzic had enough courage and trusted me enough to tell me that. It was already then that he demonstrated his dissatisfaction with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just a moment. Mr. Vukcevic, I am -- you're speaking in the same language as Mr. Zivanovic, so it's very easy for you and for Mr. Zivanovic to question and answer. But -- you don't see them, but over there, there is a team of interpreters who have to interpret every you say and Mr. Zivanovic says. And it is not instantly. It takes a little bit of time. So it is very helpful if, one, you would not speak too quickly. And, secondly, and most importantly, that you leave a little pause between Mr. Zivanovic's question and your answer. And Mr. Zivanovic has to do, of course, the same, but he knows that for a long time already. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, and I do apologise for what I've done, and I promise it will not be done again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, if I were to put the same questions to you today, the same as the ones that I put to you when this statement was compiled, including the corrections that you provided today, would your answers be the same -- sorry, let me finish, please. Would they be the same as the ones provided in this statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would tender for admission 1D2401.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D02401.1 will be Exhibit D181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, in the first four paragraphs of your statement, you described your professional career to us in quite a bit of detail. In the fifth paragraph, you said, inter alia, that you were a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia until 1990. I would like to ask you now to tell us very briefly, first of all, what this League of Communists of Yugoslavia was and what role it had at the time in the beginning of the 1990s or, rather, the end of the 1980s and the beginning of the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: This was the only political party, the only organisation, that was joined by members of the Serb people and members of other peoples as well in this complex state that was called Yugoslavia because there was no other political organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us for what reasons you ceased to be a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: The League of Communists of Yugoslavia was groping in the dark, like a blind person because of the situation that existed at the time. This vacillation, the indecisiveness of the people who represented that part had quite an effect on people who wanted to be different. Therefore, they asked to join other parties once these parties were established. Croats were increasingly joining --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting but I think we have quite a bit of transcribing problems. So could you please speak a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: I do my best, but I think fast so that's what happens. I repeat: Many people from the ranks of all the peoples of the then-Yugoslavia could hardly wait for the establishment of a party which they found to be close. What I'm saying is that Croats were increasingly joining the Croatian Democratic Community, the HDZ, and the Serbs also spontaneously started joining the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, more and more. May I just say one more thing? The HDZ was established a year before the SDS. And I remember full well the 9th of June, 1990. I lived in Beli Manastir, and that's where I'm from. On that day, buses arrived Beli Manastir. There were two or three of them, I think. They were full of youngish people who were ethnic Croats. Very loudly and in a very abrasive way, they were expressing their ethnic affiliation. This caused concern and fear amongst the Serbs who were there. Of course, I don't know the exact number, but at least half of the population was affected. Already then they were prepared to deal with the Croats who had arrived physically. They had come to establish the HDZ in Beli Manastir. In order to prevent that as much as I could, I sent two or three persons who were close to me to be near these buses and to prevent these Serbs who were so upset. I didn't want them to create any kind of incident. At the same time, I went to Vukovar by car from Beli Manastir. The distance is about 70 kilometres. On that day, the late professor, Dr. Jovan Raskovic happened to be there on that day, and that is where the founding assembly of the SDS was to be held. I would like to point out that I met Goran Hadzic then. He was in the company of the late Dr. Raskovic. Goran Hadzic and I knew each other superficially because his then wife was a student of mine, and she had already taken an exam in my subject. He walked up to me very courteously he introduced me to Jovan Raskovic, and I told him why I had come; namely, I wanted to establish the SDS in Baranja. Baranja is a region north of Osijek. And I asked him whether I had his consent. He said yes. And he told me to do that. He believed that that would be responsibly and properly. Indeed, that is what happened. So that would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Vukcevic, what was it that actually motivated you to establish this Serb Democratic Party? What were the reasons that guided you at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: A national feeling and an awareness that had been built up within me over the years by my parents and by my mother's parents. This led me and others to this party. Just like Croats joined the HDZ. Please allow me to say one more thing. We thought that loving one's own nation, one's own people, did not mean hating another people or a nation. For me, this was a humane thing, normal, justified, but in no way should one hate anybody else in order to love one's own nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement - this is the sixth paragraph of your statement, actually - you defined the HDZ not only as a national party but also as a nationalist party. So can you explain the difference to us, the difference that you saw between national and nationalist parties? Why did you believe that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Just as I said a moment ago, some people who were rushing into the HDZ, once they joined it, spoke with a great deal of intolerance, hatred even, of all others, especially the Serbs. This frightened the Serbs and perplexed them too because many of us could not believe that the persons we had been living together with all those years, we went to school together, grew up together, went to work together. We could not believe that they were so full of hatred and intolerance as they were displaying then. I repeat: I would like to say that it wasn't all Croats who were like that. That is important to point out. It was people who were trying to find their new place within this political party called the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this same statement, you said that the SDS was a national but not a nationalist party. Can you explain this to us as well, that the party was an ethnic one but not nationalist.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just as members of the HDZ displayed a great deal of intolerance and hatred towards everything that was Serbian and Yugoslav, the members of the SDS did not do that vis-à-vis non-Serbs; that is to say, Croats. And on that basis, one could see that the members of the SDS liked their own but did not hate others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, you joined the SDS in June 1990, and this is what I'd be interested in now. Do you remember that already in August 1990, some negotiations were held between the SDS, on the one hand, and the HDZ on the other as represented by Ivan Vekic then?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I personally conducted these negotiations. And this is how they started. A man named Krivic who had been a student of mine, who took his civil law exam as my student, one day, he came to see me and said, Professor, I was sent by the HDZ. I was sent to talk to you and to agree that you should organise a summit-level meeting between these parties so that we try to prevent what was in the offing. Now what was in the offing? Do I have time to speak about this a bit more extensively?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: This was the 30th of August, 1990. I remember the date very well. I also have copies of newspaper articles about this event. On the 19th of August, on a holiday which is very important for all of the Orthodox Christians, a plebiscite was held in Croatia among the Serbs. Not a referendum. The late Milan Babic was the main person among the Serbs in Croatia, and somebody gave him the idea that a referendum should be organised. I, as a lawyer and a professor of law, said the following to him, Don't say anything that stupid. That cannot be organised. That cannot be done because a referendum can be accepted or does not necessarily have to be accepted by parliament. The highest organ in a particular country, in this case, Croatia. If you want a manifestation that would express the will of the Serb people and if you call it a referendum, then those who decide about that will consider you illiterate and unprofessional. It is better for it to be called a plebiscite and you don't have to ask the parliament for approval of that. Quite simply, a form of spontaneous, social expression is organised. And at long last, the obstinate Milan Babic agreed to do that. On the 19th of August, this plebiscite was organised, it was held. And Serbs who lived in Croatia and Serbs who were born in Croatia and who lived outside Croatia expressed their views on whether they wished to live in Yugoslavia and whether we wished to have political or cultural autonomy of their own. The very next day, APCs were on the move. I don't know another name for these vehicles. These are military vehicles with a certain number of men in them. They look very threatening. They look scary. They set out to tame the Serbs. It was impossible for the Serbs to have APCs of their own to act against those APCs so what we resorted to was the forest. What do I mean? They cut trees so that they would be felled and in this way they would stop the APCs that had rubber tires. And in this way, they stopped these vehicles from reaching the areas that they had set out to reach. Of course, this provoked the Croatian authorities, and those Croatian journalists who were in favour of sensationalism called this the log revolution. Logs are very big and cannot be removed just by using one's own hands. Machinery is needed. So this happened on the 19th of August. And then the -- the plebiscite happened on that day. And the next day, the so-called log revolution took place, as I've already described it. This behaviour, again, perplexed and bothered the Croatian state and the Croatian economy. Now how and why? Because there could be no traffic. Trains could not run, vehicles could not run on roads, so then the Croatian economy and the Croatian authorities, through their party, the HDZ, started seeking a solution. How? By meeting with the representatives of the SDS and asking the representatives of the Serbs that this behaviour be stopped. And then my student Krivic, my former student who had already graduated by then came to me to my office at the law school and told me, Professor, I was sent by the HDZ to talk to you and you, in turn, to talk to Raskovic, for all of us to meet at the highest level. Very well, said I, I'll see what I can do. I don't know how all this will end up but I will do it. I called professor Jovan Raskovic who lived in Sibenik at the time on the Croatian Adriatic coast, and since we could not talk freely on the phone because we knew that that we were being listened to, every time we had to sit in the car and make the 650-kilometre long journey between Osijek and Sibenik. I told him, There is a serious matter which I need to discuss with you. Indeed, I went to Sibenik and I found him in his summer cottage. I told him what was going on and what was needed from him, and I said that I thought that that was okay. Raskovic was a smart man, and he said, Yes, I agree. You should, indeed, take part in these negotiations. But listen well: Don't go on your own. Let's go to Knin first. Let's get the people in Knin, those people who are members of the Executive Board of the party, and let them decide on your participation. Very well. Yes, very well. And then he told me, I need to tell you something else. What professor? Don't go on your own. Never go on your own. Take somebody with you. Because they can do you a lot of harm, and they can say that you said what you didn't or they can mislead you into saying what you didn't want to say. Bring somebody with you who can testify and bear witness as to what had been said. That's how I chose Boro Savic from Vukovar. That was his only role. The only activity in the negotiations.
